meta.title_plain: Why do sunflowers know how to count?
meta.teaser: One tiny adding rule hides inside sunflowers, pine cones and pineapples.

page.title: Why do sunflowers know how to count?
page.bigIdea: Add the last two numbers to get the next one: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. This simple rule, the Fibonacci sequence, hides in sunflowers, pine cones and pineapples.

cards.title: Add the last two numbers
cards.back: Each number is the two before it added together. 5 + 8 = 13, then 21, 34, 55. Like combo points in a game, it grows faster and faster.
cards.tryit: Write the first 15 numbers on paper. Check yourself: the 15th one should be 610.

cards.title: A rabbit puzzle from 1202
cards.front: Who was Fibonacci, and why did he count rabbits?
cards.back: Leonardo of Pisa travelled with his merchant dad as a boy. His 1202 book asked how fast rabbit pairs multiply. The answer was this sequence. Indian poets found it first.
cards.tryit: Each month, the new number of pairs is the last two months added. Start 1, 1 and keep going for 12 months.

cards.title: Count the spirals
cards.front: Look closely at a sunflower's middle. The seeds curl in spirals both ways.
cards.back: Sunflower seeds form two sets of spirals, often 21 and 34. Pine cones often show 8 and 13. Yet a 2016 study found 1 in 5 sunflowers break the rule.
cards.tryit: Find a pine cone, a pineapple or a sunflower photo. Count the spirals going each way. Are both Fibonacci numbers?

cards.title: The magic turn: 137.5°
cards.front: Why would a plant care about Fibonacci at all?
cards.back: Each new seed grows about 137.5° around from the last. That angle packs seeds tightly with no gaps. Change it by just a tenth of a degree, and gaps appear.
cards.tryit: Draw a dot. With a protractor, turn 137.5° and draw the next dot a bit further out. Repeat 10 times.

cards.title: Your challenge
cards.front: A staircase has 8 steps. You climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many different ways can you reach the top?
cards.back: 34 ways! Your last move is 1 step or 2 steps. So ways for 8 = ways for 7 + ways for 6. Build up: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34.
cards.tryit: Try a 4-step staircase first. List every way, like 1-1-2 or 2-2. Did you find 5?

words.d: A list of numbers that follows a rule.
A curve that winds around a centre, getting wider as it goes.
About 1.618, the number Fibonacci neighbours get closer and closer to.
About 137.5°, the turn a plant makes between one seed and the next.
A see-through half circle for measuring and drawing angles.

quiz.hint: Use the rule: look only at the last two numbers.

quiz.q: Work out 8 ÷ 5, then 13 ÷ 8, then 21 ÷ 13. What number do the answers get close to?
quiz.hint: Round each answer to one decimal place and compare them.
quiz.why: The answers are 1.6, 1.625 and about 1.615, closing in on the golden ratio, about 1.618.

quiz.q: A sunflower has 34 spirals going clockwise. Which count is most likely going the other way?
quiz.hint: Find 34 in the sequence and look at its neighbours.
quiz.why: Spiral counts are usually neighbouring Fibonacci numbers, and 55 sits right next to 34.

quiz.q: 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 12, one less than 13. Now add 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 8. What do you notice?
quiz.hint: Add carefully, then look for a Fibonacci number close to your answer.
quiz.why: The sum is 20, one less than 21, so the pattern holds again.

page.think: What if a plant turned exactly halfway, 180°, between every seed? Draw it. What would the flower look like, and why might the plant lose out?
tries: Write the first 20 Fibonacci numbers and circle the even ones. Can you spot a pattern?
